title: Trump wants to eliminate birthright citizenship before the election
description_short: Trump wants to eliminate birthright citizenship before the election
description_medium: In the weeks before the 2020 election, Donald Trump considered an executive order that would deny U.S. citizenship to children born in the country to parents who were not citizens. Reporting on the discussions said Attorney General William Barr resisted the legally contested proposal. Trump did not issue an order, and birthright citizenship remained unchanged.
description_long: In the final weeks of the 2020 campaign, Donald Trump urged people around him to consider an executive order ending birthright citizenship for children born in the United States to parents who were not citizens, according to reporting on the discussions. The proposal would have challenged the longstanding interpretation of the Fourteenth Amendment and likely faced court challenges. Attorney General William Barr reportedly opposed the plan as legally questionable, frustrating Trump. No order was issued, and the citizenship rule remained in place. The proposal mattered because it would have used presidential authority to alter a constitutional protection affecting children born in the country and, later, their eligibility to participate as citizens. The reporting does not give a precise date for the conversations or indicate that a final order was drafted. It describes a proposal discussed inside Trump’s circle, not a policy that took effect.

title: Trump names SmartBiz as first fintech to become bank
description_short: Trump names SmartBiz as first fintech to become bank
description_medium: On March 17, 2025, regulators approved SmartBiz’s acquisition of Centrust Bank NA, making SmartBiz the first fintech firm in Donald Trump’s second term to enter banking through an acquisition. The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and the Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago approved the deal. Industry observers said the decision could signal more fintech applications, though the transaction itself involved an existing bank.
description_long: SmartBiz received regulatory approval on March 17, 2025, to acquire Centrust Bank NA, a bank based in Northbrook, Illinois. The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and the Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago approved the transaction. SmartBiz described the decision as the first approval for a fintech company to become a bank during Donald Trump’s second term. The deal was an acquisition of an existing bank rather than a new charter. Fintech firms have rarely entered banking this way, and the approval prompted discussion about whether more companies might pursue similar transactions under the administration’s deregulatory approach. That possibility was a forecast, not a change in the rules or evidence of special treatment for SmartBiz. The transaction could give the company access to the advantages and responsibilities that come with a bank charter, including a different regulatory framework. Its approval is a concrete example of how regulators are handling fintech companies seeking to expand into traditional banking. The decision alone does not establish that the company received improper treatment or that other applications will be approved.

title: Trump Fires 4 Inspectors General in One Week — Retaliation for COVID Oversight
description_short: Trump Fires 4 Inspectors General in One Week — Retaliation for COVID Oversight
description_medium: In one week in April 2020, President Trump fired four inspectors general, including watchdogs connected to oversight of the COVID relief package and reports of hospital supply shortages. The dismissals drew criticism that the administration was weakening independent scrutiny while distributing emergency funds and responding to the pandemic.
description_long: President Donald Trump removed four inspectors general in a single week in April 2020. Among them were the Pentagon watchdog selected to help oversee the roughly $2 trillion COVID relief package and the Health and Human Services inspector general whose office had reported shortages of hospital supplies. Inspectors general investigate problems inside federal agencies and provide Congress and the public with independent oversight. Democrats and other critics said the timing of the dismissals suggested retaliation against watchdogs whose work could embarrass the administration. The removals came as agencies were spending emergency funds and hospitals faced intense pressure from the pandemic. Federal law required advance notice to Congress when an inspector general was removed; critics argued the administration’s actions failed to respect the purpose of that requirement. The episode raised questions about whether agency watchdogs could continue their work without fear of political retaliation. It also weakened confidence in oversight of the relief response, although the available account does not identify all four officials or establish what happened to each investigation afterward.

title: Trump: Putin sends Kirill Dmitriev to meet with Trump Campaign associate
description_short: Trump: Putin sends Kirill Dmitriev to meet with Trump Campaign associate
description_medium: On January 11, 2017, Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev and George Nader met Erik Prince in the Seychelles to discuss Russia’s interests with the incoming Trump administration. Nader later said Prince attended on Steve Bannon’s behalf. The meeting followed efforts by Dmitriev to reach members of the Trump transition team and drew scrutiny because it involved an unofficial channel for discussing U.S.–Russia policy.
description_long: Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev and George Nader met Erik Prince in the Seychelles on January 11, 2017, during the transition to Donald Trump’s presidency. Nader said Prince attended on behalf of Steve Bannon, then a senior Trump campaign figure. Dmitriev had been seeking contact with Trump transition officials and had tried to arrange meetings with Jared Kushner or Donald Trump Jr. The Seychelles meeting offered an unofficial setting to discuss Russia’s priorities with people connected to the incoming administration. Nader later described the discussion as covering what Moscow wanted from the Trump presidency. The meeting became significant because it showed an effort to establish access to the transition outside formal diplomatic channels. The participants’ presence does not by itself establish that the Trump team adopted any proposal or that the discussion led to a government decision. Dmitriev had also pursued contacts with Jared Kushner and Donald Trump Jr. before the Seychelles meeting, but no policy agreement is documented as resulting from it.

title: Donald Trump calls in to Fox News, OANN, and Newsmax
description_short: Donald Trump calls in to Fox News, OANN, and Newsmax
description_medium: On February 17, 2021, the day Rush Limbaugh died, Donald Trump called Newsmax, One America News, and Fox News to discuss Limbaugh and politics. During a Newsmax interview, Trump falsely claimed he had won the 2020 election. He also disputed President Joe Biden’s comments about the vaccine distribution plan, turning a discussion of the pandemic response into an attack on Biden.
description_long: Donald Trump called Newsmax, One America News, and Fox News on February 17, 2021, the day conservative radio host Rush Limbaugh died. He appeared twice on Fox and spoke about Limbaugh, himself, and the Presidential Medal of Freedom ceremony at the 2020 State of the Union. On Newsmax, Trump repeated the false claim that he had won the 2020 election and said some people wanted him to replace Limbaugh on conservative radio. Host Greg Kelly also asked about President Joe Biden’s statement that the prior administration had not left a vaccine distribution plan. Trump reframed the exchange as Biden claiming that no vaccine existed and called him a liar. The interviews combined a public tribute to Limbaugh with Trump’s ongoing political messaging after leaving office. His election claim contradicted the certified result, while the vaccine exchange showed how he used a question about the federal handoff to criticize Biden. The appearances did not resolve the dispute over pandemic planning, but they kept Trump’s election claims in public circulation during the transition.

title: Trump: Senate rubberstamps Trump's personal lawyer for lifetime appeals court appointment
description_short: Trump: Senate rubberstamps Trump's personal lawyer for lifetime appeals court appointment
description_medium: The Senate confirmed Emil Bove to a lifetime seat on the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit on July 29, 2025. Bove had previously worked as Donald Trump’s personal lawyer. The vote was largely along party lines, with Republican senators Lisa Murkowski and Susan Collins joining Democrats in opposition.
description_long: On July 29, 2025, the Senate confirmed Emil Bove to a lifetime judgeship on the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit. Bove had served as Donald Trump’s personal lawyer before joining the Justice Department and later being nominated to the court. Republican senators provided nearly all the votes for confirmation, while Lisa Murkowski and Susan Collins joined Democrats in opposition. Appeals court judges decide cases involving federal law and can shape legal precedent for decades, so confirmation to a lifetime seat has consequences beyond the administration that nominated them. Bove’s earlier work for Trump became part of the public discussion surrounding his nomination. The vote placed a former lawyer for the president on a federal appellate court, where he may hear disputes involving the executive branch and federal agencies. The confirmation was a Senate decision; it did not resolve the concerns raised by opponents or amount to a finding about Bove’s conduct as a lawyer. Bove’s prior work for Trump drew attention during the confirmation process, which put a former lawyer for the president on a federal appellate court.

title: Trump: New York Times calls out preferential treatment in Jeffrey Epstein case
description_short: Trump: New York Times calls out preferential treatment in Jeffrey Epstein case
description_medium: A September 2006 New York Times report examined whether Florida prosecutors gave Jeffrey Epstein preferential treatment after police pursued more serious charges than the one he ultimately faced. Palm Beach’s police chief criticized the handling of the case, and local editorial coverage questioned the decision. The article focused on prosecution choices and did not describe a role for Donald Trump.
description_long: In September 2006, The New York Times examined how Florida prosecutors handled the case against Jeffrey Epstein. Epstein had pleaded not guilty to soliciting prostitution, while Palm Beach police said they had probable cause for more serious charges involving alleged sexual offenses against minors. Instead of filing those charges directly, State Attorney Barry Krischer presented possible charges to a grand jury, which indicted Epstein on the lesser count. The Times described that approach as unusual in Florida outside capital cases. Palm Beach Police Chief Michael Reiter accused prosecutors of giving Epstein special treatment and called on Krischer to step aside. A Palm Beach Post editorial also questioned whether a wealthy, well-connected defendant had received a different kind of treatment from other suspects. The article documented contemporary criticism of the charging decision and the gap between the offenses police believed they could support and the count Epstein ultimately faced. It concerned the handling of Epstein’s case in Florida and did not describe Donald Trump’s involvement.

title: Donald Trump fires Defense Secretary Mark Esper, threatens to fire more
description_short: Donald Trump fires Defense Secretary Mark Esper, threatens to fire more
description_medium: On November 9, 2020, Donald Trump announced that he had fired Defense Secretary Mark Esper and named Christopher Miller as acting secretary. Esper had recently said he was not planning to resign. The change came days after the election and amid reports that White House personnel chief John McEntee warned staff against seeking other jobs before the administration’s transition.
description_long: Donald Trump announced on November 9, 2020, that he had fired Defense Secretary Mark Esper, making Esper the fourth official Trump had fired or demoted since Election Day, according to contemporaneous reporting. Esper told Military Times that he had not intended to resign, despite reports that he was preparing a resignation letter. Trump named Christopher Miller, then director of the National Counterterrorism Center, as acting defense secretary. Federal succession rules pointed to the deputy secretary as the next official in line, prompting questions about Miller’s appointment; the Pentagon did not comment when asked. Separately, a senior administration official said White House personnel chief John McEntee had warned staff they would be fired if they looked for other jobs. These events unfolded after Trump lost the election and before the transfer of power, when the administration still controlled the Defense Department and other agencies. The firing and reported warning added to uncertainty among officials preparing for the transition. The reports document the personnel changes and concerns they raised, but do not establish that the appointment was ruled unlawful or that every employee received McEntee’s warning.

title: Trump: FAA grants Elon Musk permission to launch 25 rockets a year
description_short: Trump: FAA grants Elon Musk permission to launch 25 rockets a year
description_medium: On May 6, 2025, the Federal Aviation Administration authorized SpaceX to launch and land rockets at its Starbase site in Texas up to 25 times a year, five times the previous limit. The decision expanded the company’s permitted flight activity at the facility. The approval attracted attention because Elon Musk’s businesses were closely associated with the Trump administration.
description_long: The Federal Aviation Administration approved a higher annual launch and landing limit for SpaceX’s Starbase facility in Texas on May 6, 2025. The authorization allowed up to 25 launches and landings per year, five times the previous limit. Starbase is used by SpaceX to test and operate its rockets, so the change expanded the number of flights the company could conduct there under the federal permit. The decision came as Elon Musk had a prominent relationship with the Trump administration and his companies were receiving federal attention across several agencies. That context prompted questions about the appearance of favoritism, but the facts available here do not show that political ties affected the FAA’s review or establish what safety conditions accompanied the increased limit. The permit is a regulatory decision with practical consequences for SpaceX’s operations and the surrounding area. Its significance depends on the terms of the authorization and the FAA’s continuing oversight of launches. The approval itself does not document a safety incident or a finding that the agency departed from its usual process.

title: Trump: The IRS gives Donald Trump a likely illegitimate $72.9 million tax refund
description_short: Trump: The IRS gives Donald Trump a likely illegitimate $72.9 million tax refund
description_medium: Donald Trump received a $72.9 million federal tax refund in 2010, along with $21.2 million in state and local refunds, according to tax records described by The New York Times. The federal refund followed years of reported business losses and included interest. Trump later showed a large Treasury payment to his lawyer Michael Cohen; the available details do not establish whether it came as one check or several payments.
description_long: In 2010, Donald Trump received a $72.9 million federal income-tax refund, as well as $21.2 million in state and local refunds, according to records examined by The New York Times. The federal payment returned taxes he had paid from 2005 through 2008, plus interest. The reporting tied the refund to large business losses Trump reported, including $1.4 billion in losses from core businesses for 2008 and 2009, which tax rules allowed him to apply against earlier income. The refund became part of a dispute with the Internal Revenue Service over the tax treatment of those losses. In 2019, Trump’s former lawyer Michael Cohen told Congress that Trump had shown him a large Treasury check and expressed surprise at the amount. The reporting did not establish whether the refund arrived as one check or as multiple payments over time, and it did not report the outcome of the IRS review or a final finding that the payment was improper. The event concerns a substantial refund and the tax dispute around it, rather than proof of illegality.

title: Trump: Israel murders Iranian scientist, protests call for Iran to attack the U.S.
description_short: Trump: Israel murders Iranian scientist, protests call for Iran to attack the U.S.
description_medium: Iranian nuclear scientist Mohsen Fakhrizadeh was killed in a targeted attack on November 27, 2020. U.S. officials and other reporting attributed the operation to Israel. The killing prompted calls for retaliation in Iran, while former CIA director John Brennan urged Tehran to wait for the incoming U.S. administration before responding.
description_long: Mohsen Fakhrizadeh, Iran’s leading nuclear scientist, was killed in a targeted attack on November 27, 2020. U.S. officials and multiple news reports attributed the operation to Israel. The attack came amid heightened tensions over Iran’s nuclear program and just weeks before Joe Biden was due to take office. Iranian protesters called for retaliation against the United States, which some believed had been involved, although the reports cited here did not establish U.S. participation. Former CIA director John Brennan urged Iran to wait for the next administration before deciding how to respond. Later reporting described a remotely operated weapon, but details of how the operation was carried out were not clear in the immediate aftermath. The killing intensified concerns about escalation and the risk of retaliatory action during a presidential transition. The killing increased pressure on Iran’s leaders to respond, while the incoming administration would soon inherit heightened tensions over the nuclear program.

title: Iran's Fordow Nuclear Facility Struck — Deepest Bunker Buster Deployed
description_short: Iran's Fordow Nuclear Facility Struck — Deepest Bunker Buster Deployed
description_medium: During the June 2025 U.S. strikes on Iran’s nuclear sites, B-2 bombers dropped 30,000-pound GBU-57 Massive Ordnance Penetrators on the underground Fordow facility. U.S. Strategic Command described the operation as the weapon’s first operational use. The strike targeted a uranium-enrichment site buried beneath a mountain near Qom; public assessments differed over the extent of the damage.
description_long: During the June 2025 U.S. operation against Iran’s nuclear facilities, B-2 bombers dropped 30,000-pound GBU-57 Massive Ordnance Penetrators on the Fordow enrichment site, according to U.S. Strategic Command. The weapon is designed to penetrate hardened underground targets, and the operation marked its first use in combat. Fordow is an enrichment facility built beneath a mountain near Qom, making it one of Iran’s most protected nuclear sites. U.S. officials described the strike as successful, while other assessments said the damage might not have completely destroyed the facility. U.S. officials described the mission as successful, but public assessments differed over how much damage the facility sustained and how long its operations would be disrupted. The use of the GBU-57 demonstrated the scale of force the United States brought to the operation and raised questions about whether military action could eliminate or only delay Iran’s nuclear capabilities. The strike formed part of a broader operation against Iran’s nuclear infrastructure, but it did not settle the future of the country’s nuclear program or the wider conflict.

title: Donald Trump taps Matt Gaetz & Tulsi Gabbard for DOJ and National Intelligence
description_short: Donald Trump taps Matt Gaetz & Tulsi Gabbard for DOJ and National Intelligence
description_medium: On November 13, 2024, President-elect Donald Trump announced Matt Gaetz as his choice for attorney general and Tulsi Gabbard for director of national intelligence. The selections placed political allies in charge of the Justice Department and the U.S. intelligence community if confirmed. They came during a series of appointments for Trump’s incoming administration.
description_long: President-elect Donald Trump announced on November 13, 2024, that he intended to nominate Representative Matt Gaetz for attorney general and selected Tulsi Gabbard to serve as director of national intelligence. The announcements were part of a rapid series of choices for the administration he was preparing to form. The attorney general leads the Justice Department, which oversees federal law enforcement and prosecutions; the director of national intelligence coordinates the work of the U.S. intelligence agencies. Trump said Gaetz would reform the department and praised Gabbard’s military service and experience in Congress. The selections drew attention because both posts carry substantial authority over law enforcement and national security. They were nominations and appointments announced by the president-elect, not evidence that either person had begun serving in the role. Gaetz later withdrew from consideration, while Gabbard’s nomination proceeded through Senate review. The choices showed the direction Trump signaled for the second administration, but their practical effect depended on confirmation and subsequent service.

title: Donald Trump: Be nice to my murderous, armed supporters as they storm your offices
description_short: Donald Trump: Be nice to my murderous, armed supporters as they storm your offices
description_medium: After armed demonstrators entered Michigan’s Capitol to protest COVID-19 restrictions in May 2020, President Trump called them “very good people” and urged Governor Gretchen Whitmer to negotiate. The protesters had threatened police and Whitmer. Trump’s post followed weeks of criticism from him and his allies over the state’s public-health measures.
description_long: On May 1, 2020, President Donald Trump publicly backed demonstrators who had entered the Michigan State Capitol while protesting COVID-19 restrictions. Some carried firearms, and the protesters had threatened police officers and Governor Gretchen Whitmer. Trump called them “very good people,” said they were angry and wanted their lives back, and urged Whitmer to “give a little” and make a deal. The post followed weeks of criticism from Trump and his allies over the state’s pandemic rules. His response gave national attention to an armed confrontation inside a state capitol and pressed an elected governor to negotiate with the demonstrators. The tweet came as officials were trying to contain the coronavirus and enforce restrictions on public activity. Trump’s praise and call to negotiate gave national attention to an armed protest directed at elected officials and law enforcement during a dispute over emergency health measures.

title: Trump: Channel 4: Trump campaign had data on 200 million voters, targeted Black voters in 2016
description_short: Trump: Channel 4: Trump campaign had data on 200 million voters, targeted Black voters in 2016
description_medium: A Channel 4 News investigation reported that the 2016 Trump campaign and its partners held data on nearly 200 million Americans. About 3.5 million Black voters were placed in a “Deterrence” category used for digital ad targeting. The campaign denied targeting Black voters, and the investigation noted that no complete archive showed which users saw particular ads.
description_long: A Channel 4 News investigation published in September 2020 examined how the Trump campaign, the Republican National Committee, and Cambridge Analytica used voter data during the 2016 election. The investigation said the operation held digital information on nearly 200 million Americans and placed about 3.5 million Black voters in a category called “Deterrence.” Campaign material in the investigation suggested that some ads were intended to reduce support for Hillary Clinton. The campaign denied deliberately targeting Black voters. Channel 4 also noted that many political ads were distributed as temporary Facebook posts, so no complete public archive showed exactly which voters received them. The findings raised concerns about the use of personal data to discourage participation among a specific group of voters. They documented the campaign’s audience categories and strategy, while leaving uncertainty about the delivery and reach of individual ads. The case became part of a wider debate about political microtargeting, voter suppression, and the transparency of online campaigning.

title: Trump Withdraws from Paris Agreement and Pauses WTO Contributions
description_short: Trump Withdraws from Paris Agreement and Pauses WTO Contributions
description_medium: On January 20, 2025, Donald Trump ordered the United States to begin withdrawing from the Paris Agreement and revoked the U.S. International Climate Finance Plan. The United Nations issued a withdrawal notice a week later. That spring, the administration also paused contributions to the World Trade Organization and stopped negotiations on the World Health Organization’s Pandemic Agreement.
description_long: On January 20, 2025, Donald Trump signed an executive order directing the United States to withdraw from the Paris Agreement for a second time. The United Nations issued a formal notice on January 27, beginning the process of withdrawal. Trump also revoked the U.S. International Climate Finance Plan, ending commitments intended to help developing countries address climate change. In March, the administration paused U.S. contributions to the World Trade Organization for 2024 and 2025 and halted negotiations on the World Health Organization’s Pandemic Agreement. The decisions affected several forms of international cooperation: climate policy, trade institutions, and pandemic planning. The Paris Agreement withdrawal did not take effect immediately, and the WTO funding pause was a separate action from the treaty process. Together, the moves signaled a reduced U.S. role in multilateral initiatives after the administration had previously participated in them. They prompted concern among partners about whether the United States would continue supporting international agreements and institutions. Taken together, the decisions marked a retreat from several forms of multilateral cooperation, though each affected a different institution and followed its own process.

title: Trump's Doha Agreement Sets Stage for Taliban Takeover of Afghanistan
description_short: Trump's Doha Agreement Sets Stage for Taliban Takeover of Afghanistan
description_medium: The February 2020 Doha Agreement committed the United States to withdraw its forces from Afghanistan by May 2021 in exchange for Taliban counterterrorism assurances. The Trump administration negotiated directly with the Taliban without Afghanistan’s elected government and agreed to release 5,000 Taliban prisoners. President Biden completed the withdrawal in August 2021, and the Afghan government collapsed within days.
description_long: The Doha Agreement, signed by the Trump administration and the Taliban in February 2020, set a timetable for the withdrawal of U.S. forces from Afghanistan by May 2021. In return, the Taliban promised not to allow terrorist groups to use Afghan territory. Afghanistan’s elected government was not a party to the agreement, and the deal included the release of 5,000 Taliban prisoners. President Biden carried out the final U.S. withdrawal in August 2021; the Afghan government collapsed soon afterward as the Taliban took control. The agreement shaped the commitments and political conditions that the next administration inherited. Critics argue that excluding Kabul from negotiations weakened the Afghan government and that releasing prisoners strengthened Taliban forces. The agreement did not itself determine every event in 2021, and Biden made the final decision to complete the withdrawal. The agreement shaped the commitments and political conditions inherited by the next administration, while the relative influence of the deal and Biden’s later withdrawal remains debated.

title: Trump Pardons All Jan 6 Defendants Including Seditious Conspiracy Convicts
description_short: Trump Pardons All Jan 6 Defendants Including Seditious Conspiracy Convicts
description_medium: On January 20, 2025, Donald Trump issued pardons or commutations for nearly all defendants charged or convicted in connection with the January 6 Capitol attack. The clemency included people convicted of seditious conspiracy, among them leaders of the Proud Boys and Oath Keepers. Families of injured officers and other critics condemned the decision.
description_long: On his first day back in office, January 20, 2025, President Donald Trump issued pardons or commutations covering nearly all people charged or convicted in connection with the January 6, 2021 attack on the U.S. Capitol. The clemency applied to more than 1,500 people, including members of the Proud Boys and Oath Keepers convicted of serious offenses such as seditious conspiracy. Some sentences were commuted, while other defendants received full pardons and pending cases were dismissed. Families of officers injured during the attack expressed outrage, and critics said the sweeping action sent a message that political violence carried out in Trump’s name would be forgiven. The pardons removed or reduced criminal consequences for people whose cases arose from an effort to disrupt Congress’s certification of the 2020 election. The decision did not erase the historical record of the attack, but it changed the legal consequences for those covered. The White House proclamation distinguished commutations from full pardons and dismissed pending cases; the people covered had different roles and convictions.

title: Trump Attacks General Milley, Suggests He Could Be Executed for Treason
description_short: Trump Attacks General Milley, Suggests He Could Be Executed for Treason
description_medium: In September 2022, former President Trump called General Mark Milley’s post–January 6 calls with his Chinese counterpart “treasonous” and wrote that the offense “used to be” punishable by death. Milley was chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff. Defense officials and legal experts condemned the post as dangerous rhetoric toward a senior military officer.
description_long: In September 2022, Donald Trump attacked General Mark Milley on Truth Social over calls Milley had made to his Chinese counterpart after the January 6 Capitol attack. Trump described the calls as a “treasonous act” and said treason “used to be” punishable by death. Milley was serving as chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff and had made the calls during a period of concern about the stability of U.S. decision-making. Defense officials and legal experts criticized Trump’s language as dangerous to civil-military relations. The post was not a government order or a legal proceeding, and Milley was not charged with treason. It nonetheless directed death-penalty rhetoric at a senior officer for conduct carried out in an official role. The comments intensified scrutiny of Trump’s attacks on military and government officials who had crossed him. The episode illustrates the risks of political leaders using criminal accusations and execution language against public servants, particularly when those remarks can encourage threats against them or their families.

title: Trump Pressures VP Pence to Reject Electoral Votes on January 6
description_short: Trump Pressures VP Pence to Reject Electoral Votes on January 6
description_medium: In the weeks before January 6, 2021, President Trump pressed Vice President Mike Pence to reject or delay the counting of electoral votes for Joe Biden. Trump claimed Pence could return contested votes to the states, though the vice president had no such authority. Pence refused and said the Constitution did not permit him to overturn the result.
description_long: In the weeks before Congress met to count electoral votes on January 6, 2021, Donald Trump and his allies urged Vice President Mike Pence to reject or delay votes that confirmed Joe Biden’s victory. Trump argued that Pence could send votes from contested states back to their legislatures, but the vice president had no constitutional power to do so. On the morning of January 6, Trump publicly criticized Pence for refusing and repeated the demand at the Stop the Steal rally shortly before the attack on the Capitol. Pence released a letter explaining that his role in the certification process was ministerial and did not give him authority to choose which votes to count. The pressure campaign targeted the formal transfer of presidential power and placed Pence at the center of a constitutional crisis. His refusal allowed Congress to resume certification after the attack. Trump’s demand sought to turn Pence’s limited role in counting the votes into a means of changing the election outcome.

title: Ivana Trump Rape Allegation in 1990 Divorce Deposition — Later Recanted Under Legal Pressure and NDA
description_short: Ivana Trump Rape Allegation in 1990 Divorce Deposition — Later Recanted Under Legal Pressure and NDA
description_medium: During the Trumps’ 1990 divorce, Ivana Trump described a 1989 sexual encounter in a deposition. Journalist Harry Hurt III published the allegation in a 1993 book. Ivana later said she had not used “rape” in a literal or criminal sense, and in 2015 called the story “totally without merit.” Donald Trump denied it.
description_long: During the Trumps’ 1990 divorce, Ivana Trump described a 1989 sexual encounter in a deposition. The allegation became public through Harry Hurt III’s 1993 book, *Lost Tycoon*, which drew on a copy of the deposition. Ivana’s 1993 statement said that she had used the word “rape” to describe feeling violated but did not mean it in a literal or criminal sense. In 2015, after the Daily Beast revisited the account, she said the story was “totally without merit” and described herself and Donald Trump as close friends. Trump denied the allegation. title: Trump Pressure Triggers Wave of State Voter Suppression Laws Ahead of 2026 Midterms

Florida, Mississippi, Utah, South Dakota, and Wyoming passed laws requiring documentary proof of citizenship to register — documents that half of U.S. citizens do not possess. Five Republican-controlled states eliminated grace periods for late-arriving mail ballots after Trump's EO called for it. Florida state Rep. Jenna Persons-Mulicka said her proof-of-citizenship bill fully answers the president's call; Wyoming Secretary of State Chuck Gray said his state's measure was key in supporting President Trump's pivotal work. title: Election Lawyer Fundraising Scheme - Grifting 'Stop the Steal'

description_medium: From November 2020 through January 2021, Trump’s fundraising operation raised more than $250 million while appealing to supporters who believed donations would fund legal challenges to the election result. description_long: Donald Trump and his legal team ran a massive fundraising scheme around their 'Stop the Steal' election fraud claims, raising over $250 million from supporters for legal challenges that were largely nonexistent or frivolous while pocketing most of the money for other purposes. The scheme involved sending hundreds of fundraising emails claiming donations would fund crucial legal battles to overturn the election, when in reality most of the money went to Trump's political action committee and other non-legal expenses. Small-dollar donors believing they were funding legitimate legal challenges instead subsidized Trump's post-presidency political operation and personal expenses. The fundraising appeals used increasingly desperate language about stolen elections and urgent deadlines, extracting money from supporters who trusted Trump's claims about widespread fraud. Many of the promised legal challenges never materialized, while those that were filed were quickly dismissed by courts for lack of evidence. The scheme exploited Trump's most loyal supporters, including elderly Americans and those on fixed incomes who made repeated small donations believing they were saving democracy. Internal Trump campaign communications revealed that officials knew many fraud claims were false but continued raising money off them anyway. The 'Stop the Steal' fundraising operation represented one of the largest political fundraising frauds in American history, converting election lies into personal profit while deceiving millions of Americans about the integrity of the democratic process.

description_long: Donald Trump's Securities and Exchange Commission voted to abandon defense of climate-related disclosure rules that required publicly traded companies to report greenhouse gas emissions and climate risks, eliminating corporate accountability for environmental impact while implementing Project 2025's systematic destruction of climate transparency. Acting SEC Chairman Mark Uyeda declared the climate disclosure rule 'deeply flawed' and harmful to the economy, withdrawing the agency's legal defense and yielding oral argument time back to federal courts challenging the requirements that had taken over two years to develop. The systematic destruction of climate accountability mechanisms violated investor protection principles by denying shareholders access to material information about climate risks that could affect company valuations and long-term viability, while creating information asymmetries that favored corporate secrecy over market transparency. The SEC's abandonment of climate disclosure represented implementation of Project 2025's vision to eliminate environmental regulations and corporate accountability, prioritizing short-term industry profits over investor protection and climate transparency that financial markets increasingly demanded.

description_long: The Trump administration granted Dan Gertler a one-year special license easing U.S. sanctions on January 15, 2021. description_long: On July 1, 2025, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau terminated its consent order against mortgage servicer Fay Servicing and waived alleged noncompliance. The decision reduced federal oversight of a servicer regulators had previously found out of compliance with mortgage rules. description_long: Donald Trump published *The America We Deserve* on January 15, 2000, with journalist Dave Shiflett credited as co-author. His description complicates how the book should be read as a statement of Trump’s own policy views: it appeared under Trump’s name and was associated with a possible campaign, while the credited co-author later said he was the sole writer. The book publicly linked those ideas to Trump in 2000, though Shiflett’s later account leaves open how much Trump shaped its contents. Shiflett’s later account also raises questions about the extent of Trump’s authorship. The publication remains notable as an early example of Trump using a book to introduce political positions before running for office.

description_long: During the first presidential debate of 2020, moderator Chris Wallace asked Donald Trump to condemn white-supremacist groups and right-wing militias. The exchange came weeks before the election, as Trump was already casting doubt on mail voting and the eventual result. His statements raised concerns about election administration and whether the president would respect a peaceful transfer of power. The Proud Boys’ public repetition of the phrase made the exchange a defining moment in the campaign debate over militia politics, voter intimidation, and Trump’s willingness to accept the result.

description_long: Michael Caputo began working in Moscow in 2000 for Gazprom Media, a subsidiary of the Russian state energy company Gazprom. Later that year, after Caputo returned to the United States, Roger Stone encouraged him to move to Miami Beach and start a public-relations firm. title: Trump Recognizes Moroccan Sovereignty over Western Sahara for Abraham Accords
description_short: Trump Recognizes Moroccan Sovereignty over Western Sahara for Abraham Accords
description_medium: In December 2020, the Trump administration recognized Moroccan sovereignty over Western Sahara as part of Morocco’s agreement to normalize relations with Israel. The decision reversed longstanding U.S. policy on the disputed territory. The Polisario Front and Algeria condemned the move, which critics said bypassed the Sahrawi people’s right to determine the territory’s status.
description_long: On December 10, 2020, the Trump administration recognized Moroccan sovereignty over Western Sahara as part of an agreement in which Morocco would normalize relations with Israel. The proclamation reversed longstanding U.S. policy on the territory, which Morocco had taken control of in 1975 and whose status remains disputed. United Nations resolutions had called for a referendum on self-determination for the Sahrawi people. The Polisario Front, which represents Sahrawi interests, and Algeria condemned Washington’s decision. Human-rights groups and international-law scholars criticized the recognition, arguing that it rewarded Morocco without allowing the territory’s population to choose its political future. The administration linked the policy change to a diplomatic agreement in the Abraham Accords framework, making Western Sahara’s status part of a broader effort to normalize relations between Israel and Arab states. The U.S. proclamation changed Washington’s position, but it did not resolve the dispute or replace the promised referendum. The decision raised questions about whether diplomatic recognition of contested territory could be exchanged for progress on a separate regional agreement.

title: Donald Trump requests a mail-in ballot for Florida election after months of lies
description_short: Donald Trump requests a mail-in ballot for Florida election after months of lies
description_medium: On March 5, 2021, Donald Trump requested a mail ballot for a Palm Beach County election after months of criticizing mail voting during the 2020 campaign. It was reportedly his third ballot request in the county. Because the mailing deadline had passed, the ballot had to be collected in person; the available reporting did not confirm who picked it up or whether Trump voted.
description_long: Former President Donald Trump requested a mail ballot for a Palm Beach County election on March 5, 2021, after repeatedly making false claims about widespread fraud in mail voting during the 2020 campaign. The request was reportedly his third in the county. The deadline to have a ballot mailed had passed, but voters could still request one and collect it in person through the following Tuesday. The Palm Beach Post reported that an associate likely picked up Trump’s ballot, as had happened for earlier elections, but did not confirm who collected it or whether he voted. Trump’s request drew attention because he used a method he had attacked publicly while his party pursued restrictions on mail voting in other states. The contrast illustrated how his criticism was political rather than a rejection of the method for his own use. Requesting a ballot was allowed under Florida’s election procedures and did not itself violate a rule. Trump’s ballot request was reported, but it was not confirmed who collected it or whether he voted.

title: Trump: Roger Stone launches Stop The Steal to funnel money to his American Greatness PAC
description_short: Trump: Roger Stone launches Stop The Steal to funnel money to his American Greatness PAC
description_medium: Roger Stone registered Stop The Steal as a tax-exempt political organization on April 6, 2016, and transferred $50,000 to it from his Committee to Restore American Greatness PAC. The new group paid $20,000 to Jensen & Associates. In July, Stop The Steal transferred $63,000 back to Stone’s PAC, prompting questions about how it reported and used its funds.
description_long: Roger Stone registered Stop The Steal as a tax-exempt political organization on April 6, 2016, listing Sarah Rollins as the registrant. That day, Stone transferred $50,000 from his Committee to Restore American Greatness PAC to the new group, which then paid $20,000 to Jensen & Associates. On July 12, Stop The Steal transferred $63,000 back to the PAC. The organization’s tax filings did not clearly explain how it accumulated the larger amount after reporting few intervening donations and expenses. Its website directed online contributions to Stone’s PAC before and after the separate organization was formed. Stop The Steal used its name to solicit money around claims that elections had been rigged, including the 2016 Republican primary. These transactions raised questions about financial transparency and whether donors understood which entity would receive their contributions. The transfers and unclear filings raised questions about financial transparency, but they did not by themselves establish unlawful conduct. The event concerns the organization’s formation and movement of funds, rather than the later 2020 Stop the Steal campaign.

title: Trump: I'll lift sanctions on Russia if they cut down on nukes (which changes nothing)
description_short: Trump: I'll lift sanctions on Russia if they cut down on nukes (which changes nothing)
description_medium: In a January 2017 interview with The Times of London, Donald Trump said he would consider lifting sanctions on Russia if it reduced its nuclear arsenal. Russian political scientist Andrey Piontkovsky criticized the idea, arguing that limited disarmament could create diplomatic theater without reducing the broader security risk. The proposal linked sanctions policy to arms control shortly before Trump took office.
description_long: In an interview published on January 15, 2017, Donald Trump said he would offer to lift sanctions on Russia if Moscow reduced its nuclear weapons stockpile. Russian political scientist Andrey Piontkovsky criticized the proposal, arguing that a limited reduction could be presented as disarmament while leaving the broader strategic balance unchanged. He described arms-control negotiations as a diplomatic game and warned that Russia might gain sanctions relief without materially reducing the danger posed by its nuclear arsenal. The discussion came as Trump had also called for expanding U.S. nuclear capability and Vladimir Putin had said Russia would respond in kind. Trump’s statement was a conditional offer, not a signed agreement or a change to the sanctions then in place. The exchange raised questions about whether sanctions imposed for other reasons should be tied to nuclear reductions and how such a bargain could be verified. Piontkovsky’s criticism was an expert opinion, not proof that every arms-control agreement would be ineffective. No evidence in this episode shows that Russia accepted the proposal or that sanctions were lifted as a result.

title: USAID Dismantled — Ends Humanitarian Programs in 90 Countries Including Childhood Vaccination
description_short: USAID Dismantled — Ends Humanitarian Programs in 90 Countries Including Childhood Vaccination
description_medium: In February 2025, the Trump administration placed most USAID direct-hire employees on administrative leave and began a reduction in force affecting about 2,000 U.S.-based staff. The move accompanied the termination of foreign-assistance contracts and disrupted programs in more than 90 countries. A federal judge temporarily blocked parts of the shutdown, finding the administration had likely acted unlawfully.
description_long: In February 2025, the Trump administration sharply reduced the operations of the U.S. Agency for International Development. USAID said most direct-hire employees would be placed on administrative leave, and about 2,000 U.S.-based workers faced a reduction in force. The administration also terminated thousands of foreign-assistance contracts affecting programs in more than 90 countries. USAID-supported work included emergency food aid, clean water, disaster relief, disease response, and childhood vaccination. Reporting described interruptions to immunization programs and the end of long-running polio work in Pakistan that had been associated with former Secretary of State Colin Powell’s USAID legacy. A federal judge temporarily blocked parts of the shutdown, finding that the administration had likely acted unlawfully. The cuts raised concern about continuity of health and humanitarian services for people who depended on them and about the ability of remaining staff to monitor programs overseas. The agency’s staff and activities contracted sharply, though the court order and continuing operations meant that not every USAID function ceased at once.

A New York court suspended his law license in 2021 after finding that he had made false statements, while a Washington, D.C., disciplinary case continued. description_long: New York’s Appellate Division suspended Rudy Giuliani’s law license in 2021 after finding that he had made false statements about the 2020 election. A disciplinary proceeding in Washington, D.C., continued during 2022. A federal judge in Michigan also sanctioned Giuliani and other Trump lawyers for election-related lawsuits, while Dominion Voting Systems and Georgia election workers Ruby Freeman and Shaye Moss pursued defamation claims over false accusations. These were separate proceedings with different allegations and outcomes. Giuliani’s election claims had consequences beyond politics: they were tested in court, led to professional discipline, and caused individuals who were accused of fraud to seek legal remedies. The license suspension was a professional-discipline decision, separate from the defamation cases brought by Dominion Voting Systems and the Georgia election workers. The Michigan sanction addressed the lawyers’ filing of election claims that the court found baseless.

title: Senate Acquits Trump — Romney Only Republican to Vote to Convict
description_short: Senate Acquits Trump — Romney Only Republican to Vote to Convict
description_medium: On February 5, 2020, the Senate acquitted President Trump on both articles of impeachment. Mitt Romney was the only Republican to vote for conviction on abuse of power; the Senate also rejected the obstruction-of-Congress article. Republican leaders had blocked witnesses and additional documents, and Trump later used the acquittal in campaign messaging.
description_long: On February 5, 2020, the Senate voted to acquit President Donald Trump on both articles of impeachment arising from his dealings with Ukraine. The abuse-of-power article failed 52–48, with Republican Senator Mitt Romney joining Democrats to vote for conviction. The obstruction-of-Congress article failed 53–47. Romney said Trump was guilty of an appalling abuse of public trust, becoming the first senator to vote to convict a president of his own party. Republican leadership had blocked efforts to hear from additional witnesses and obtain documents offered by career officials and impeachment witnesses. Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell also coordinated with the White House on trial strategy. Trump called the investigation a hoax and later invoked the acquittal at campaign events. The vote ended the Senate trial without removing Trump from office. The proceedings raised questions about whether the Senate had fully examined the allegations when witnesses and documents were withheld. Romney’s vote showed that at least one Republican senator considered the conduct serious enough to warrant conviction. The outcome was a constitutional decision by the Senate, not a criminal judgment.

title: SAVE Act Passes House, Requiring Documentary Proof of Citizenship to Vote
description_short: SAVE Act Passes House, Requiring Documentary Proof of Citizenship to Vote
description_medium: The House passed the SAVE Act on April 10, 2025. The bill would require documentary proof of U.S. citizenship before states could process voter registrations for federal elections and would create private lawsuits and criminal penalties for election officials who failed to comply. The measure still needed Senate approval and had not become law.
description_long: On April 10, 2025, the House of Representatives passed H.R. 22, the Safeguard American Voter Eligibility Act, by a 220–208 vote. The bill would amend the National Voter Registration Act to require documentary proof of U.S. citizenship before a person could register for federal elections. Acceptable documents could include a passport or qualifying identification. The bill also required states to establish procedures for removing noncitizens from voter rolls and allowed private lawsuits against election officials who registered applicants without the required proof. It included criminal penalties for registrars who did not comply. The measure tracked requirements in President Trump’s March executive order, which sought to impose similar rules without congressional approval. Voting-rights advocates warned that eligible citizens who lack easy access to documents could face barriers, including people whose names differ from official records after marriage. House passage was only one step in the legislative process; the bill still required Senate action and was not yet in force. The proposal raised questions about citizenship verification, voter access, and liability for the local officials who administer elections.

title: NIH Terminates ~2,500 Research Grants, Cuts $5 Billion in Funding
description_short: NIH Terminates ~2,500 Research Grants, Cuts $5 Billion in Funding
description_medium: Between January and June 2025, the Trump administration terminated about 2,500 NIH research grants worth nearly $5 billion, according to Senator Patty Murray. A JAMA analysis counted 694 cancellations totaling $1.81 billion through April 8. A federal judge later ruled that grant cancellations tied to perceived DEI connections violated federal law.
description_long: Between January and June 2025, the Trump administration terminated about 2,500 National Institutes of Health grants totaling nearly $5 billion, according to Senator Patty Murray. A JAMA analysis of the period from February 28 through April 8 identified 694 cancellations worth $1.81 billion, including nearly $506 million from the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases. The cancellations affected research grants that the administration associated with diversity, equity, and inclusion. On June 16, a federal judge in Boston ruled that NIH had acted unlawfully by arbitrarily canceling more than $1 billion in grants on that basis, finding that the policy disproportionately harmed people of color and LGBT people. The administration also pushed out thousands of NIH employees and proposed reducing the agency’s budget by $17 billion, or 38 percent. The JAMA figure covers a shorter period than the broader estimate, so the totals measure different windows and should not be added together. Grant cancellations disrupted ongoing research, while the court ruling established that at least part of the cancellation policy violated federal law. The budget reduction remained a proposal, not an enacted cut.

title: CFPB Gutted: 90% of Consumer Protection Bureau Staff Eliminated
description_short: CFPB Gutted: 90% of Consumer Protection Bureau Staff Eliminated
description_medium: In February 2025, acting CFPB director Russell Vought halted supervision and examinations and closed the bureau’s headquarters. By April, about 1,500 of roughly 1,700 employees were slated for termination, an attempted cut of nearly 90 percent. A federal judge blocked the shutdown in March, finding the bureau was close to dismissing its entire staff.
description_long: The Trump administration and the Department of Government Efficiency moved to sharply reduce the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau in 2025. Acting Director Russell Vought ordered supervision and examination work halted on February 9, closed the bureau’s headquarters, and set its funding to zero. By April 17, roughly 1,500 of the agency’s 1,700 employees were slated for termination, an attempted cut of nearly 90 percent. The reductions threatened an agency created after the 2008 financial crisis to oversee consumer finance and address predatory lending. Internal employee testimony described a plan to reduce the CFPB to “a room at Treasury with five men and a phone.” A federal judge blocked parts of the shutdown on March 28, finding the bureau was within hours of firing nearly all of its staff. The court intervention means the proposed workforce reduction should not be described as fully completed. The record also notes that Elon Musk’s companies had matters before consumer regulators, raising questions about a possible conflict as DOGE targeted the agency. The episode concerned regulatory independence and consumer protection, while litigation limited the administration’s effort to close the bureau.

title: SNAP Food Stamp Cuts: 2.7 Million Lose Benefits Under OBBBA
description_short: SNAP Food Stamp Cuts: 2.7 Million Lose Benefits Under OBBBA
description_medium: The One Big Beautiful Bill Act, signed July 4, 2025, reduced projected federal SNAP spending by more than $280 billion over ten years. CBO estimates projected that expanded work requirements would mean 2.4 million fewer recipients in an average month, with another 300,000 losing benefits when state cost-sharing begins in 2028. The law also capped future benefit growth.
description_long: The One Big Beautiful Bill Act enacted on July 4, 2025 imposed the largest cuts to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) in the program's history, reducing federal SNAP spending by over $280 billion over ten years. CBO analyses released in August 2025 found that expanded work requirements will cause 2.4 million fewer Americans to receive benefits in an average month, including parents of dependent children newly subject to work mandates for the first time. An additional 300,000 people will lose benefits beginning in 2028 when states are required to share benefit costs, with some states expected to leave the program entirely. A cap on Thrifty Food Plan updates will reduce the average monthly benefit from a projected $227 to $213 by 2034. Groups most at risk include veterans, people experiencing homelessness, and young adults aging out of foster care.

title: CECOT Torture Pipeline: Trump Ships 252 Venezuelans to El Salvador Dungeon
description_short: CECOT Torture Pipeline: Trump Ships 252 Venezuelans to El Salvador Dungeon
description_medium: In March 2025, the Trump administration used the Alien Enemies Act to send about 238–252 Venezuelan men to El Salvador’s CECOT prison, under a reported $6 million agreement. The transfers proceeded despite a federal court order and with little due process. Human Rights Watch and Cristosal later documented beatings, sexual abuse, isolation, and denial of food and medical care in detention.
description_long: On March 15-16, 2025, the Trump administration invoked the 1798 Alien Enemies Act to deport 238-252 Venezuelan migrants to El Salvador's Terrorism Confinement Center (CECOT) megaprison, paying the Bukele government $6 million for a one-year renewable term. The U.S. government flew deportees with little or no due process, defying a federal court order by Judge James Boasberg. A November 2025 joint report by Human Rights Watch and Cristosal, based on interviews with 40 of the detainees, documented systematic beatings, sexual abuse, solitary confinement as punishment, incommunicado detention, denial of adequate food and medical care, and conditions that drove detainees to the brink of suicide. Investigators found many deportees had no criminal record in the U.S. or abroad, and the groups concluded the U.S. was complicit in torture, enforced disappearances and other violations. The men were eventually returned to Venezuela in a prisoner swap after months of imprisonment.

title: Hegseth Signal Chat: Classified Yemen Strike Plans Leaked
description_short: Hegseth Signal Chat: Classified Yemen Strike Plans Leaked
description_medium: In March 2025, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth shared plans for U.S. strikes against Houthi targets in Yemen through a personal Signal chat that included Atlantic editor Jeffrey Goldberg. The messages disclosed aircraft launch times, strike windows, and missile timing drawn from a CENTCOM communication. The disclosure raised operational-security and federal records concerns.
description_long: In March 2025, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth used his personal cell phone to share sensitive operational details about planned US airstrikes against Houthi targets in Yemen via the commercial Signal messaging app — accidentally including Atlantic editor-in-chief Jeffrey Goldberg in the chat. The messages disclosed F/A-18 launch times, bomb drop schedules, drone strike windows, and Tomahawk missile timing — information drawn directly from a classified SECRET//NOFORN email sent by CENTCOM commander Gen. Michael Kurilla. Hegseth shared the same information in a second Signal chat that included his wife and brother. A December 2025 Pentagon Inspector General report found Hegseth violated Defense Department regulations and federal records law, concluding his actions created a risk to operational security that could have resulted in failed U.S. mission objectives and potential harm to U.S. pilots. The Pentagon refused to provide Hegseth's phone to investigators; many messages had auto-deleted. Trump officials including DNI Tulsi Gabbard and CIA Director John Ratcliffe denied classified material was shared.

title: US Strikes IRGC Targets After Iran Attacks US Base in Jordan
description_short: US Strikes IRGC Targets After Iran Attacks US Base in Jordan
description_medium: On July 29, 2026, U.S. Central Command said it struck dozens of Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps targets in Iran after attempted Iranian missile attacks on U.S. forces. The BBC reported that Iran said three people, including a child, were killed. The strikes came amid a widening conflict and a breakdown of the June ceasefire.
description_long: On July 29, 2026, following an Iranian ballistic missile attack on a US military base in Jordan that the IRGC framed as retaliation for US airstrikes killing Iranian advisers in Iraq, US Central Command launched what it described as a heavy wave of strikes against Iran, hitting dozens of IRGC targets over approximately two hours. The targets included military command centers, missile and drone production and storage facilities, coastal surveillance and defense sites, and maritime capabilities along the Strait of Hormuz. In a coordinated operation, the US partnered with Saudi Arabia to strike Iran-backed militias in Iraq, killing at least 20 fighters and 6 Iranian IRGC advisers. Trump vowed to hit Iran very hard before the strikes, publicly telegraphing the retaliation to media. The Jordan attack by Iran came as the fragile June 17 ceasefire agreement was already breaking down over repeated Strait of Hormuz confrontations. CENTCOM reported all Iranian missiles targeting US forces were intercepted. The strikes represented the latest escalatory cycle in a conflict with no clear diplomatic off-ramp, raising fears of an open-ended US military engagement.

title: Congress Defunds Corporation for Public Broadcasting, CPB Shuts Down
description_short: Congress Defunds Corporation for Public Broadcasting, CPB Shuts Down
description_medium: The Corporation for Public Broadcasting announced on August 1, 2025, that it would wind down after Congress rescinded $1.1 billion in funding through fiscal year 2027. CPB had distributed federal support to more than 1,500 public radio and television stations. Its president, Patricia Harrison, said the closure was the first in the corporation’s nearly 60-year history.
description_long: In May 2025, Trump signed an executive order directing the Corporation for Public Broadcasting to cease all direct and indirect funding to NPR and PBS, calling their journalism biased and not fair. On July 24, 2025, Trump signed a $9 billion rescissions bill that clawed back $1.1 billion in congressionally appropriated CPB funding through fiscal year 2027. CPB, which had channeled federal money to over 1,500 local public radio and television stations nationwide for nearly 60 years, announced on August 1, 2025 that it was beginning to wind down operations. CPB President Patricia Harrison called it the first time in nearly six decades Congress had refused to fund the corporation. NPR, PBS, and their more than 1,500 member stations — many serving rural communities with no commercial news alternatives — faced devastating funding gaps. The FCC simultaneously investigated NPR and PBS for alleged commercialization violations under Chairman Carr. Approximately 50 million Americans already lived in news deserts in 2025 according to the Medill Local News Initiative. NPR pledged $8 million from its budget to help local stations. The shutdown represented the most comprehensive government elimination of public broadcasting infrastructure in U.S. history, undertaken as critics argued it was designed to silence journalism hostile to the administration.

title: Press Freedom Collapse - U.S. Ranking Falls to 57th Place
description_short: Press Freedom Collapse - U.S. Ranking Falls to 57th Place
description_medium: Reporters Without Borders ranked the United States 57th in its 2025 World Press Freedom Index, its lowest position since the index began more than 20 years earlier. The organization said Trump’s return to office worsened conditions. The Committee to Protect Journalists separately warned that early executive actions were creating a chilling effect and restricting journalists’ access.
description_long: Under Donald Trump's presidency and return to power, the United States fell to 57th place in global press freedom rankings - the lowest position since Reporters Without Borders began publishing its index over 20 years ago, with Trump's attacks on media 'greatly exacerbating the situation.' The U.S. press freedom ranking plummeted from 32nd place in 2013 to 45th by the end of Obama's presidency, then crashed to 55th during Trump's first term before hitting the historic low of 57th place under his second presidency. The Committee to Protect Journalists released an unprecedented early report titled 'Alarm bells: Trump's first 100 days ramp up fear for the press, democracy' after determining that press freedom was 'no longer a given in the United States.' CPJ's Katherine Jacobson said Trump's 'flurry of executive actions' created 'a real chilling effect and have the potential to curtail media freedoms' through access restrictions, FCC investigations of major networks, and systematic attacks on press credibility. The dramatic decline reflected Trump's systematic campaign against media freedom, including calling journalists 'enemy of the people,' celebrating reporter injuries, and using government power to investigate news outlets that criticized him. International press freedom organizations warned that the U.S. was losing its status as a global leader in press freedom while providing a model for authoritarian leaders worldwide to justify their own media crackdowns.

title: Fox News Coordination - State TV Propaganda Machine
description_short: Fox News Coordination - State TV Propaganda Machine
description_medium: Court filings in Dominion Voting Systems’ defamation case exposed a gap between Fox News’ private doubts and its public coverage of Trump’s 2020 election claims. Sean Hannity testified that he did not believe the fraud allegations, even as Fox hosts promoted them to viewers. The case ended in a $787.5 million settlement.
description_long: Donald Trump transformed Fox News into a state propaganda network through coordinated messaging, regular phone calls with hosts, and mutual promotion of election lies that the network's own stars admitted they never believed. Depositions in the Dominion Voting Systems lawsuit revealed that Fox News personalities, including Sean Hannity, privately acknowledged Trump lost the 2020 election while publicly promoting his false fraud claims to their millions of viewers. Hannity testified under oath that he 'did not believe it for one second,' while Fox executive Meade Cooper confirmed she 'never believed the lies about Dominion.' Despite their private skepticism, Fox News hosts amplified Trump's election conspiracy theories for months, presenting them as credible to maintain their audience and support Trump's attempts to overturn the election. The coordination between Trump and Fox News created an alternate reality where millions of Americans believed false claims about voting machines, dead people voting, and massive fraud that never occurred. Trump would often live-tweet Fox News shows, turning them into interactive propaganda sessions where hosts would adjust their coverage based on his real-time feedback. The relationship was so close that Fox News personalities served as unofficial advisors to Trump, with hosts like Sean Hannity regularly consulting on policy and political strategy. The Dominion lawsuit exposed how Fox News knowingly broadcast false information about voting systems, leading to a $787 million settlement and revealing the network's willingness to spread lies for profit and political influence.

title: Family Separation Policy Expansion - 'Pathway to Mass Deportations' Through Child Detention
description_short: Family Separation Policy Expansion - 'Pathway to Mass Deportations' Through Child Detention
description_medium: Project 2025 proposed expanding immigration enforcement, including longer detention for children and fewer services for mixed-status families. Human Rights Watch separately documented lasting harm from the family-separation policy used in 2018. Whether the second Trump administration implemented each measure remains unclear; proposed changes and earlier practice are distinct from current policy.
description_long: Donald Trump systematically expanded family separation policies as a 'pathway to mass deportations and family separation' by ending the Flores settlement agreement to detain children in jail-like conditions, eliminating benefits for unaccompanied minors while transferring their care from Health and Human Services to Department of Homeland Security for large-scale detention. The comprehensive family destruction program represented implementation of Project 2025's plan to reject 'America's historic commitment to family unity in the immigration system' while using child detention as a weapon to deter immigration and terrorize mixed-status families where some members have citizenship or legal status. The systematic targeting included barring mixed-status families from federally subsidized housing, prohibiting college students who are not citizens from receiving student loans, and denying ALL students loans if they attend schools offering in-state tuition to undocumented students, creating educational apartheid based on immigration status. Trump's expansion eliminated restrictions on ICE operations in sensitive zones like schools and hospitals while deputizing police officers and National Guard troops from Republican-led states to assist in raids that deliberately separated families as a deterrent strategy. The family separation apparatus violated international humanitarian law and constitutional due process protections while inflicting deliberate trauma on children and families, with Human Rights Watch documenting that 1,360 children had never been reunited with parents six years after the original Trump-era separations. The systematic family destruction represented what advocates called 'violent, xenophobic attack on immigrants' that used child detention and family trauma as tools of immigration enforcement while eliminating due process protections and humanitarian safeguards that had prevented government-sanctioned child abuse.

title: EPA Research Division Elimination - 1,155 Scientists Terminated and $748.8 Million Cuts
description_short: EPA Research Division Elimination - 1,155 Scientists Terminated and $748.8 Million Cuts
description_medium: In July 2025, EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin announced plans to eliminate the Office of Research and Development, affecting about 1,155 scientists and reducing the agency’s workforce by a projected 23 percent. Reuters reported expected savings of $748.8 million. The office’s research informed EPA rules on chemicals, wildfire smoke, and drinking-water risks.
description_long: Donald Trump's EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin announced elimination of the agency's entire Office of Research and Development, terminating 1,155 scientists including chemists, biologists, and toxicologists while cutting the workforce by 23% to achieve $748.8 million in savings that prioritized budget reduction over environmental protection and public health. The EPA research elimination continued Trump's broader assault on environmental science, with the agency having already terminated more than two dozen Environmental Justice and External Civil Rights staffers through Reduction In Force notices that cited executive orders on 'Ending Radical and Wasteful Government DEI Programs' and 'Department of Government Efficiency Workforce Optimization.' The scientific capacity destruction violated federal environmental protection obligations by eliminating research capabilities needed to assess health risks and regulate toxic substances, while the Heritage Foundation's Project 2025 had specifically criticized the EPA's science office as promoting environmental regulations that faced opposition from chemical manufacturers and various industries. Trump's research elimination created dangerous regulatory gaps where environmental rules could no longer be supported by independent scientific assessment, effectively ending the agency's ability to establish evidence-based protections against environmental hazards while prioritizing industry interests over public health and environmental safety. The systematic scientific destruction represented what environmental advocates called 'devastating blow to environmental protection' that would leave Americans vulnerable to toxic exposure while eliminating research capabilities that had protected public health for decades.

title: Trump: Louis DeJoy: We destroyed the USPS mail sorting machines
description_short: Trump: Louis DeJoy: We destroyed the USPS mail sorting machines
description_medium: On September 21, 2020, a federal judge ordered the Postal Service to reverse changes that threatened election-mail delivery. USPS had to prioritize ballots, pre-approve overtime during the peak voting period, and submit a plan to restore service. The agency said more than 700 high-speed sorting machines had already been dismantled and could not be returned to operation.
description_long: Federal judge Victor Marrero ordered the U.S. Postal Service on September 21, 2020, to address operational changes that could delay election mail. The order required USPS to treat ballots and other election mail as first-class or priority mail, pre-approve overtime requested from October 26 through November 6, and file a plan to restore timely delivery. The ruling followed service delays after Postmaster General Louis DeJoy reduced overtime and processing capacity. USPS told the court that more than 700 high-speed sorting machines had been dismantled for parts and could not be restored. Another judge had questioned whether the removal of machines was concentrated in counties that voted for Hillary Clinton in 2016. The orders came weeks before the presidential election, when states depended on the Postal Service to deliver ballots and election materials. The court sought to protect that delivery as the agency responded to operational problems. The record does not establish that every delay was intentional, but the loss of processing equipment limited USPS’s ability to reverse the changes quickly.

title: Trump officials include journalist in confidential military strike chat

The chat discussed operational planning for the coming days. Goldberg was not an intended participant, and his inclusion exposed internal deliberations to a journalist through a personal messaging app.
description_long: National Security Adviser Michael Waltz created a Signal group called “Houthi PC small group” in March 2025 to coordinate policy and operations involving Yemen’s Houthis. He added Atlantic editor Jeffrey Goldberg, who was not an intended participant, and messages about the coming 72 hours appeared in the chat. Waltz asked officials to identify staff contacts for follow-up coordination. The group included senior administration officials and used a commercial messaging service rather than an authorized government system for confidential deliberations. Goldberg later described receiving the messages, bringing attention to the group’s purpose and membership. The disclosure raised concerns about how sensitive national-security planning was handled and whether officials followed recordkeeping and communications rules. The chat concerned coordination around upcoming operations; a separate entry describes the detailed strike plans Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth shared. Goldberg’s accidental inclusion exposed the discussion to an outside reporter, but the account does not show that he interfered with the military operation or that the leak changed its outcome. The episode prompted scrutiny of both the group’s security practices and the administration’s use of commercial apps for official business.

The event raises questions about how private business with a foreign government intersects with a former president’s political influence and family relationships.
