title: Donald Trump & friends illegally transfer $130,000 to Stormy Daniels
description_short: Donald Trump & friends illegally transfer $130,000 to Stormy Daniels
description_medium: Stormy Daniels received $130,000 in October 2016 in exchange for staying silent about an alleged 2006–2007 affair with Donald Trump. Trump’s lawyer Michael Cohen arranged the payment through a shell company. Cohen later said a check for the payment bore Donald Trump Jr.’s signature and pleaded guilty to campaign-finance violations connected to the transaction.
description_long: Stormy Daniels received $130,000 in October 2016 in exchange for keeping quiet about an alleged affair with Donald Trump in 2006–2007. Trump’s lawyer Michael Cohen arranged the payment through Essential Consultants LLC, a company he formed weeks before the election. Cohen later testified that a check used to reimburse him was signed by Donald Trump Jr. and presented a copy during a 2019 congressional hearing. In 2018, Cohen pleaded guilty to campaign-finance violations connected to the Daniels payment and a separate payment to Karen McDougal. Trump initially denied knowing about the arrangement and later acknowledged reimbursing Cohen. The timing of the payment, shortly before the election, led to questions about whether it was intended to keep damaging information from voters. Cohen’s guilty plea concerned his role in the payments; it did not by itself establish every participant’s intent. The transaction became part of later criminal proceedings in New York involving Trump’s business records. The episode links the campaign’s response to personal allegations with the legal risks of disguising political spending as private reimbursement.

title: Trump's impeachment team replaced by Russian and Israeli mafia attorney
description_short: Trump's impeachment team replaced by Russian and Israeli mafia attorney

description_long: Five attorneys left Donald Trump’s impeachment defense team less than two weeks before his Senate trial in February 2021. Butch Bowers, Deborah Barbier, Josh Howard, Johnny Gasser, and Greg Harris departed after a disagreement about strategy, according to a person familiar with the decision. Trump wanted the lawyers to argue that widespread election fraud had deprived him of the presidency, while the attorneys had been preparing to focus on whether the Senate could try a president after he left office. Trump then named David Schoen and Bruce Castor to lead the defense. Schoen had represented Roger Stone and met Jeffrey Epstein before Epstein’s death; he had also discussed representing people he described as Russian and Israeli organized-crime figures. That history does not establish that Schoen or his clients committed crimes. The departures left the new team with little time to prepare for a trial about Trump’s role in the January 6 attack. The episode highlighted a clash between Trump’s election claims and the legal arguments his departing lawyers were willing to make.

title: Trump: State Dept. moves to support sex trafficking, genocide, and extremism
description_short: Trump: State Dept. moves to support sex trafficking, genocide, and extremism
description_medium: The State Department laid off 1,353 employees in July 2025 as part of office closures. Many affected roles supported work on human trafficking, genocide, violent extremism, and women’s rights. The department’s trafficking office had lost about 70 percent of its staff, and its annual report on trafficking was not released by its deadline.
description_long: The State Department closed offices and laid off 1,353 employees in July 2025, including staff whose work concerned human trafficking, authoritarianism, genocide, violent extremism, and women’s rights. The Office to Monitor and Combat Trafficking in Persons was established with bipartisan support about 25 years earlier to address sex and labor trafficking and publish an annual report on conditions around the world. Its 2025 report was due June 30 but had not appeared by the time of the cuts. The department’s trafficking office had lost roughly 70 percent of its staff since Trump took office, leaving about 35 employees, many of whom were told they would be reassigned. An official quoted anonymously by Mother Jones said the office had been “decimated.” The reductions prompted concern that the department would have less capacity to track trafficking and other human-rights abuses overseas. The changes did not amount to U.S. support for trafficking or genocide; they reduced staffing and reporting in offices responsible for monitoring those issues. The consequences depend in part on whether remaining staff can continue the office’s investigative and reporting work.

title: Donald Trump calls local news, uses 9/11 as a promotional opportunity
description_short: Donald Trump calls local news, uses 9/11 as a promotional opportunity

description_long: On the morning of the September 11, 2001 attacks, Donald Trump called New York television station WWOR/UPN 9 to comment on the unfolding events. He discussed the skyline and his 40 Wall Street building, saying it had been the second tallest building in lower Manhattan before the World Trade Center was built and was now the tallest. When asked what people should do, Trump told viewers they would have to “never forget.” The interview included both a response to the national emergency and remarks about his real-estate holdings. Trump was not involved in rescue operations, and the interview did not affect the response to the attacks. It became notable because he brought attention to his property while appearing on local television during a moment of national grief. The broadcast preserves his words and the way he framed the event in the immediate aftermath of the attacks, without speculation about his motives beyond what he said on air.

title: Trump: Intel: Russia is interfering in the election next week and after
description_short: Trump: Intel: Russia is interfering in the election next week and after

Officials said Russian actors had breached state and local networks, potentially giving Moscow wider access to voting infrastructure. They expected further activity could sow doubt if results were delayed or Trump lost.
description_long: U.S. intelligence officials warned in October 2020 that Russia posed a greater threat to election security than Iran and might interfere during and after election week in ways that could benefit Donald Trump. Officials said Russian actors had recently breached state and local computer networks, potentially giving Moscow broader access to voting infrastructure. They expected that if the presidential race remained unresolved on election night, Russian groups could deface websites, release nonpublic information, or take other actions to sow confusion about the results. The reporting also said officials believed Russia might support Republican efforts to dispute the outcome if Trump lost. Some intelligence officials accused Director of National Intelligence John Ratcliffe of downplaying the threat but did not identify specific actions he had taken. The warnings came shortly before the 2020 election, when confidence in election administration was already under strain. They described anticipated interference and network-access risks, not evidence that Russia changed votes or that every predicted action occurred. The episode showed that intelligence agencies expected a foreign campaign to exploit uncertainty around the count and the peaceful transfer of power.

description_long: On April 15, 2025, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth had senior adviser Dan Caldwell escorted from the Pentagon after Caldwell was identified during an investigation into leaks. The episode raised questions about how leak investigations were conducted and whether the accusation against Caldwell had been established before he was escorted from the building. The distinction between a charge, an ongoing inquiry, and a proven disclosure matters in assessing why a senior adviser lost access to the Pentagon.

title: Trump: Howard Rubenstein to Kushner: Buy a paper, buy a building, marry rich
description_short: Trump: Howard Rubenstein to Kushner: Buy a paper, buy a building, marry rich
description_medium: After Charles Kushner went to prison in March 2005, Jared Kushner sought advice from publicist Howard Rubenstein on rebuilding the family’s image. description_long: Charles Kushner went to prison on March 4, 2005, after pleading guilty to tax evasion, witness tampering, and illegal campaign donations. Jared Kushner later sought advice from New York lawyer and publicist Howard Rubenstein about rebuilding the family’s image and protecting Jared’s future. A family friend quoted in the account said Rubenstein recommended buying a newspaper, buying a prominent Manhattan building, and marrying into a wealthy family. Jared later acquired the New York Observer, purchased 666 Fifth Avenue, and married Ivanka Trump. The sequence connects three parts of his public life—media ownership, real estate, and marriage—but does not show that each happened solely because of Rubenstein’s advice. Rubenstein’s clients included high-profile business figures such as Rupert Murdoch and Jeffrey Epstein. His suggestion came years before Jared Kushner entered Donald Trump’s political orbit as a senior adviser. The episode offers a glimpse of how the younger Kushner approached the family’s public standing after his father’s conviction, while the later business and personal decisions had their own circumstances and motivations.
